Will the Mnister of  URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any pr oposal to develop more rain

(c) the funds proposed to be allocated towards the same; and 
(d) whether Government realize the seriousness of harvesting rain water 
and how Government propose to educate the various municipal corporations 
in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI O. 
RAJAGOPAL): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha 
Statement 
(a) to (d) The Ministry of Water Resources has reported that the Central 
Ground Water Board (CGWB) under that Ministry has implemented a 
Central Sector Scheme for 'Study of Recharge to Ground Water' during Ninth 
Five Year Plan. Under the Scheme, artificial recharge projects were taken up 
in the country, including in some Metro cities, the details of which are given 
in the Annexure. [See Appendix 197 Annexure no. 4] 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri K. Rahman Khan. 
13 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2002] 
The CGWB has proposed a Central Sector Scheme on "Development of 
Ground Water Resources and Rain Water Harvesting in Majo r Cities" at an 
estimated cost of Rs. 20.00 crore for inclusion in the Tenth Five Year Plan. 
17 major capital cities, viz. Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai. Kolkata, Hyderabad, 
Guwahati, Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Bhubaneshwar. Jaipur, Lucknow, 
Bhopal, Patna, Raipur, Ranchi, Thiruvananthapuram and Chandigarh are 
proposed to be included in this scheme. This proposed scheme is still at a 
consultation stage. 
The CGWB has prepared  and circulated Manual and Guidelines on 
Artificial Recharge to Ground Water to all States/Union Territories 
incorporating various modern techniques of rain water harvesting for 
adoption. The Board also organi zed mass awareness and training 
programmes on rain water harvesting all over the country. A website oh Roof 
Top Rain Water Harvesting (www. cgwb india.com) has also been launched 
to make aware and educate the public about various techniques of harvesting 
rain water and store it for future us e. The Board also provides technical 
guidance to Individuals/organizations/ in dustries to adopt efficient recharge 
system through out the country. 
The Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty Alleviation has also 
circulated the literature/guidelines on rain water harvesting provided by the 
Ministry of Water Resources/CGWB to all State/UT Chief Secretaries and 
Secretaries in-charge of urban water supply for adoption in those areas where 
there has been sharp decline in the ground water level. State Governments 
have also been advised to make a beginning in the existing Government 
offices/buildings housing complexes and to make it mandatory for all new 
building by amending the building bye-laws. In Delhi, the Ministry has 
issued a notification on 28.7.2001 for modification/addition in the building 
Bye-laws, 1983 which makes it mandatory for water harvesting through 
storing of water runoff including rain water in all new buildings on plots of 
100 sq. mtrs and above.

*87. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether It has come to the notice of Government that an independent 
survey conducted by a prom inent national daily, r ecently throws up several 
disturbing facts about the quality of drinking water supplied to various parts 
of the Capital; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
30 

[25 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) whether it is a fact that the sample of Delhi Jal Board has failed in the 
test conducted by the All India Institut e of Medical Sciences also leading to 
an outbreak of typhoid amongst its doctors; and 
(d) if so, the preventive and remedial steps proposed in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION (SHRI ANANTH KUMAR): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Delhi Jal Board has reported that the amount of Total Dissolved 
Solids (TDS) and Total Hardness in the water supplied by It are well within 
permissible limits prescribed by the Bureau of Indian Standards {IS-10500-
1993) and by the Central Public Health and Environmental Engineering 
Organisation (CPHEEO), Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty 
Alleviation, Govt, of India. The water is adequately disinfected and free 
Chlorine residual at level of 0.2 to 0.5 mg/1 is maintained at the consumer's 
end. 
(c) Delhi Jal Board is supplying filtered water in bulk to AIIMS. The 
AltMS authorities are mixing water from tubewells locally installed and 
operated by them. 
The News-item in this regard appeared in the Hindustan Times dated 
1.9.2002. Consequently the matter was investigated by Director {Treatment 
and Quality Control), Delhi Jal Board. A total of 120 samples were lifted and 
water of all the samples was found to be having sufficient free residual 
chlorine. 
(d) Delhi Jal Board is taking following preventive and remedial 
steps to provide potable water:— 
(i) Regular surveillance of quality of water is done by lifting and 
testing the water samples right from raw water Intake upto 
consumer's end. About 300 winter samples are lifted daily and 
tested by Six well-equipped Laboratories. 
(ii) 140 MGD Water Treatment Plant is being set up at Sonia Vihar 
Trans Yamuna Area and targeted to be completed by December, 
2003 
(iii) A regular survey is being d one to replace old corroded/ leaking 
water mains. 
Delhi Jal Board has replaced 114 Kms. Length of water lines In 
the year 1999-2000, 208 Kms. In 2000-2001, and

*89. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that a disgusting mixture of smoke and fog 
(smog) is keeping pollutants, especially suspended particulate matter and 
pollen at breathing level, causing widespread viral infection, Asthma etc. in 
most parts of North and some parts of Western India; and 
(b) if so, the measures, so far, take n or are being contemplated by 
Government so that this health hazar d environment could be controlled and 
adequate medical care in the shape of prevention and treatment is taken? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI 
SHATRUGHAN SINHA): (a) It has been a general observation that during 
the winter season, including the smoggy conditions, the levels of Suspended 
Particulate Matter (SPM) are comparatively 
37 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2002] 
higher than during the other seasons. The SPM affects the respiratory system 
and may cause Asthma and viral infection. Studies conducted by Vallabha 
Bhai Pate! Chest Institute. New Delhi, and National Institute of Occupational 
Health, Ahmedabad, have shown some relationship between air pollution and 
respiratory diseases. 
(b) The present health care infrastructure  at the Centre and State levels is 
geared to meet the needs of the pe ople suffering from viral infections. 
Asthma etc. However, as part of pr eventive measures, the Government has 
already Implemented certain control measures such as introduction of:—

and

THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING {SHRI VED PRAKASH GOYAL): (a) to 
(c) The term state-of-the-art system to monitor ship traffic is 
49 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2002] 
usually applied to the system that monitors ship traffic to ensure safe navigation 
of ships at Port channels. Vessel Traffi c Management System (VTMS) is a radar 
surveillance system broadly intended for providing effective guidance to pilotage 
of incoming and outgoing vessels. The radar surveillance system has a 
communication network with centers of Port activities controlling traffic 
movement. The system is designed to identify a medium-sized vessel, to compute 
the positional fixings along the shipping channel, to track all targets, mobile and . 
stationary, which are automa tically projected in th^scr een. to compute mobile 
target speed, course and absolute movement along the shipping channel and to 
forecast expected time of arrival and u pdate all Information every second with 
access to and from the different control points. 
VTMS facilities are presently availabl e at Kolkata, Mumbal, Jawahar Lai 
Nehru, Mormugao and New Mangalore Ports. The installation of VTMS at 
Kandia Port has been taken up in the Gulf of Kutch, jointly by this Port, Gujarat 
Maritime Board and the Directorate General of Lighthouses and Lightships. 
Paradip Port has decided to take up the installation of VTMS during the 10"^ Plan 
period considering the level of traffic in the Port and cost involved. The facility of 
VTMS has not been felt necessary at Visakhapatnam, Chennai, Cochin, Tuticorin 
and Ennore Ports.

and procedures on the basis of the advice and recommendations of expert 
bodies, like the Law Commission, the Malimath Committee etc. 
Further, the Government have also been constantly reviewing the 
accumulation of arrears in courts. Besides, increasing the judge-strength from 
time to time, the Government have set up/encouraged alternative modes of 
dispute-resolution, including conciliation, mediation and arbitration. Special 
tribunals, like Central Administrative Tribunal, State Administrative Tribunals 
Income Tax Appellate Trib unal, Labour Courts etc. have been set up to 
expedite disposal of cases. Inform ation Technology is being used in 
generation of cause list, providing

information to the litigants/advocates et c. for speedy disposal of cases. Pilot 
project for the district courts has been started for computerization of city civil 
courts in the four major metro cities of Delhi, Chennai, Kolkata and Mumbai. 
All Central Ministries/ Departments have  been requested to take necessary 
steps like review of Acts/laws, administered by them, filing of counter-
affidavit in time and avoidance of unnecessary adjournment of cases. 
Fast Track Courts have been set up for quick disposal of long pending 
cases, priority being accorded to sessi ons cases pending for 2 years or more 
and cases involving underthals in jails. 
Civil Procedure Code has been amended and the amendments have been 
brought into force w.e.f. 1.7.2002, which include limit the number of 
adjournments which can be granted to a party to three, provide for speedy 
process service by speed post, courier se rvices, FAX or Email, authorize the 
court to fix time limit for oral arguments and provide for a number of other 
measures aimed at ensuring expeditious disposal. 
The Minister of Law & Justice has been addressing the High Courts 
periodically for filling up of vacancies of Judges in the Hi gh Courts. Efforts 
are also being made to adopt alternative modes of dispute resolution, such as, 
arbitration, conciliation and settlement of cases through Lok Adalats.

New patent regime 
457. SHRI R PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
captioned, "Patent regime unlikely to benefit developing nations: UK 
58 

(25 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Report", which appeared in the Economic Times, dated the 20"^ September. 
2002; 
(b) if so. the details thereof and Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) the details of steps Government propose to take with regard to the 
n^ajor problems highlighted in the report so as to adequately safeguard the 
interests of the developing countries esoeeially India in the new patent 
regime? 
THE fyllNISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN SINGH): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. The 
Commission on Intellectual Property Rights was set up by the British 
Government with a view to  consider (a) how nation al intellectual property 
regimes could best be designed to benefit developing countries within the 
context of internationa l agreements, including the agreement on Trade 
Related Aspects of Intellectual Property; (b) how the international 
framework of rules and agreements might be improved and developed; and 
(c) the broader policy framework needed to complement intellectual property 
regimes. 
The report which seeks to integrate intellectual property rights and 
development policy, neither negates nor invalidates the utility of the 
intellectual property system per se for developing countries. 
It does, however, emphasise the need for adequate safeguards in the 
patent laws of developing countries. The main safeguards suggested in 
respect of patent regimes relate to: compulsory licensing; parallel imports; 
Government use of patent; exclusion of diagnostic, therapeutic and surgical 
methods from patentability; exclusion of new uses of known products from 
patentability; Bolar provision; prohibition of patent protection on plants and 
animals including genes and genetically modified plants and animals; and an 
obligation to disclose the geographical source of the genetic resources used 
in invention in the patent applications. The Patents Act, 1970 as amended by 
the Patents (Amendment) Act, 2002 substantially provides for these 
safeguards along with provisions which, in sum, enable an appropriate, 
timely and efficient response to national and public interest 
requirements/concerns.

464.   SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN: 
SHRI V.V. RAGHAVAN: 
W\[\ the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state:

plantation commodities tea, coffee and rubber, the import of the commodities 
for re-export has not affected the do mestic industry for the reasons given

  * In the case of tea, M/s. Hindustan Lever Ltd., which is also a 100% 
Export Oriented Unit (EOU), is the only multinational company

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE {SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) Regulation of the 
production of the Genetically Modified Crops Including environmental 
release has been laid down under statutory provision of Environmental 
Protection Act, 1986. Under the rule of the manufacture, use, Import and 
Storage of Hazardous Mi ro-organisms/Genetically Engineered Organizers or 
cell, 1989 notified under the Environmental Act, 1986 food s t u f f ,  
ingredients in food stuffs and additives including processing aids containing 
or consisting or genetically engineered organisms or cells shall not be 
produced, sold, imported or used except with the approval of the Genetic 
Engineering Approvals Committee- 
The Genetically Modified products that  are currently in the international 
market have to pass risk assessment conducted by national authorities of the 
countries where they are permitted. As per the WHO, the safety assessment 
of Genetically Modified foods generally investigate (a) direct health effects 
(toxicity); (b) tendencies to provoke allergic reaction (allergenicity): (c) 
specific components thought to have nutritional or toxic properties; (d) the 
stability of the inserted gene; (e) nutri tional effects associated with genetic 
modification; and (f) any unintended effects which could result from the gene 
insertion. 
All genetically modified foods are evaluated for health risk. The Maize 
variety "Starlink" developed in the USA was one such genetically Modified 
crop that was withdrawn from the market in USA and Japan because of 
suspected health risk. In India only BT cotton has been permitted, after 
extensive tests and risk assessments, to be commercially produced and 
marketed.

Dear Shri 
As you are kindly aware, Central Government adopted the National 
Population Policy in February 2000 with an objective of achieving stable 
population, nationally, by 2045. For attaining this objective it is necessary to 
achieve certain socio-demographic indicators by 2010, 
108 

[25 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
which will pave the way for stable population. Among the major goals for 
2010 are:— 
1. To meet the demands in full for basic reproductive and child 
health services, supplies and infrastructure. 
2. Reducing infant mortality rate to below 30 per 1000 live births. 
3. Reducing maternal mortality to below 100 per one lakh live 
births. 
4. Achieving universal immunization of children against all vaccine 
preventable diseases. 
5. Achieving 80% institutional deliveries and 100% deliveries by 
trained persons. 
6. Increasing use of contraceptives w ith a wide basket of choices.
  
7. Achieving 100% registration of births, deaths, marriages and 
pregnancies 
8. Integrating Indian system of Medicines  in providing 
reproductive and child health services. 
9. Promoting small family norm to achieve replacement levels of 
fertility by 2010. 
 
10. Making school education up to age 14 free and compulsory and 
reduce drop out at primary and secondary school levels. 
11. Promoting delayed marriage for girls. 
12. Bringing about convergences in im plementation of related social 
sector programmes so that fami ly welfare becomes a people's 
centered programme. 
To achieve the above goals emphas is should be laid on focused 
campaigns, evolving good management practices and strengthening 
provision of services and supplies at the grass roots level. Effective 
decentralization of services to Panchayat Raj bodies involvement of NGOs 
and private sector in creation of awareness and effecting service delivery are 
essential strategies which need to be adopted by the States. 
Since, there are vast disparities among the States in the achievement of 
the ssocio-demographic indicators, the strategies for 
109 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2002] 
implementation of the programmes have to be different. Some States like 
Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Goa have already achieved replacement level of fertility. 
They have to devise programmes for sustainability and enhanced investment 
in human beings for improving the quality of lives that people lead. On the 
other hand, States like Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, 
Chattisgarh, Jharkhand and Orissa have to implement the programmes of 
family welfare and reproductive and child health more vigorously, in order to 
increase the outreach of supplies and services for promoting small family 
norm. The Central Government has set up an Empowered Action Group to 
assist these States (Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Orissa, 
Uttaranchal, Jharkhand and Chattisgarh), which have, so far, lagged behind, 
in socio-demographic achievements in devising focused programmes for 
improving the situation there. 
Some of the State Governments like Andhra Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya 
Pradesh, R^asthan and Gujarat have al ready formulated th eir State specific 
population policies and other State Governments have initialed action for 
developing their population policies. This is a welcome step. This reflects the 
commitment of the State Governments towards population stabilization and 
sustainable development. 
It may be noted in this conext that National Population Policy affirms the 
commitment of the Government towards voluntary and informed choice and 
consent of citizens while availing re productive health care services and 
continuation of target free approach in  administering family welfare services. 
The,NPP-2000 provides a policy framework for advancing goals and 
prioritizing strategies during the next decade, to meet the reproductive and 
child health needs of the people of India and to achieve net replacement levels 
by 2010. It is based upon the need to simultaneously address issues of child 
survival, immunization, maternal hea lth and contraception while increasing 
outreach and coverage of a comprehensive package of reproductive and child 
health services by Government, industry and the voluntary, Non-Government 
sector, working in partnership. Impos ing arbitrary targ ets on contraception 
like sterilization, lUDs etc. reflects a 'topdown' approach, which goes against 
decentralized planning and service delivery and denies people the right to 
informed choice. Instead, a Community Needs Assessment Approach which 
aggregates the level of expectations of performance from the field into an 
achievable and quantified goal will be a more suitable strategy for population 
stabilization. 
110 

[25 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
In view of these basic principles, the National Population Policy does not 
provide for any individual  incentives or disincenti ves, because incentives 
always look small and distort response of citizens while on the other hand 
disincentives tend to be coercive. It has also been noticed that the 
disincentives always hit the poor and down trodden especially those who 
belong to scheduled castes and tribes and backward classes much harder than 
the privileged sections of society. Till the large unmet needs of those socially 
backward groups for health and family welfare services are met, proposing 
and puritive measures is clearly irrational. Similarly making a two-child 
norm conditional for welfare measures  deprives these very sections 
disproportionately for whom these sche mes are meant. The disincentives are 
also anti-women since women in our country do not enjoy the freedom to 
decide how many children they would like to bear. Debarring such women 
from contesting elections or from public employment opportunities makes a 
mockery of policies to empower women, Further, it will provide an impetus 
for sex-selective abortions and female feticide, worsening the already 
deplorable sex ratio in some parts of the country. 
t would therefore, request you that while formulating State specific 
population policies, the State Government may kindly keep the conceptual 
framework of National Population Policy in view. Those States which have 
included coercive measures and disincentives in their State Population 
Policies may undertake a review of their Policy documents to bring them in 
line with the National Population Policy, 2000, with regard to the strategies 
for population stabilization. The Policy is based on the commitment for 
improving the quality of lives that people lead without any coercion or 
controlling the option of the citizens. In this regard, you may like to take the 
help of National Level Resource Committee constituted by this Department. 
A copy of the Order relating to his Committee is enclosed. 
As Population Policy is an issue of vital concern for the overall socio-
economic development of the States and is  not merely a health related issue, 
I would request you to assume a leadership role in formulation of the policy 
framework. 
I am enclosing an article of Prof. Amartya Sen, Noble Laureate and a note 
prepared by us on two-child norm and on incentives and disincentives, which 
you may find useful. 
Yours faithfully, 
(SHATRUGHAN SINHA)

514. SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU): Will the Minister 
of HEALTH AND FAMILY.,WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a new technique for curbin g infertility among couples named 
ROSNI (Round Spermatid Nuclear Injection) has been developed, in the field 
of Test Tube Baby Technique and Artifi cial Reproductive Technology at the 
Jaipur Fertility and Microsurgery Research Centre; 
(b) if so, the details of the technique and how far it has tested to be 
successful; and 
(c) the steps being taken to promote the technique? 
117 

 
RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2002] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) "ROSNI" or Round 
Spermatid Nuclear Injection Technique is a new technique in the field of test 
tube baby and this artificial reproductive technology has been developed at 
Jaipur Fertility and Microsurgery Research Centre. ROSNI offers alternative 
solutions for men with non-obstructive azoosoermia and testicular foci of 
spermatogenesis up to round spermatid stage. In this technique, the eggs are 
retrieved from female partner, after ovulation induction under transvaginal 
sonography guidance, like any routine In Vitro Fertilisation (IVF) procedure. 
At the same time, testicular issue is taken from husband and round spermatids 
(haploid) nuclei are extracted from if and injected directly in to the oocytes tike 
intracytoplamic sperm in jection (ICSI) technique. The fertilized egg or 
embryo is transferred back to uterus on day 3 of retrieval. Confirmation of 
pregnancy is done by blood test (S. BhCG) after 15 days. 
However, the fertilization rate as well as pregnancy rate (about 5%) using 
round spermatids is far less than that reported by conventional "Test Tube 
Baby Technique". Moreover, the safety of using round spermatozoa in this 
technique is still being debated. Some  reports suggest th at the spermatids 
{recovered from patients with complete  spermiogenesis failure) are often 
deficient in the factor(s) responsible for oocyte activation which could result 
in abnormal fertilization and the impairment of preimplantation and post-
implantation development of foetus. Besides this, there are other reports which 
have also expressed concern about th e possible health hazards for children 
resulting from the use of spermatids for assisted reproduction. 
The first report of success by this proc edure came in 1995 (Tesarik et al, 
1995 Tesarik & Mendoza, 1996). However, this technique has not been 
universally accepted and certain countr ies have banned this technique, e.g. 
U.K. 
In the light of the available data, it is essential to go slow in using the 
technique ROSNI to treat infertility.

Guidelines for Foreign Investment in Indian entities 
GUIDELINES FOR; 
(i) PUBLICATION OF INDIAN EDITIONS OF FOREIGN 
ECHNICAL/SCIENTIFIC/SPECIALITY MAGAZINES/ 
JOURNALS/PERIODICALS; AND 
142 

[25 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(ii)  FOREIGN INVESTMENT IN INDIAN ENTITIES  UBLISHING 
SCIENTIFIC/TECHNICAL/SPECIALITY MAGAZINES/ 
JOURNALS/PERIODICALS 
PREAMBLE 
The Union Government has decided to allow: 
(i) Publication of Indian editions of foreign scientific, technical and 
speciality magazines/periodicals/journals: and 
(ii) Foreign investment upto 74% in Indian entitles publishing 
scientific/technical and speciality magazines/periodicals/ 
journals. 
1. Application 
(i)   An application shall be made to the Ministry of Information & 
Broadcasting in the prescribed format to determine the I      nature 
of contents of the publication.

Broadcasting, payable at New Delhi.

proposed publication is covered under the category of scientific, 
technical or speciality magazine/periodlcal/journal.

of the Press and Registration of Books Act and Rules 
made there under for publication of the foreign journal;

a copy of which would'be sent to RNI/SIA/RBI and the 
applicant.

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2002] 
(ii) Determination of category assigned to the publication (s) is liable 
for review by the Ministry of i&B if the contents of the

KRISHNAMURTHY): (a) and (b) There is no general Central law governing 
all the communities on compulsory registration of marriages. However, those 
who choose to register their marriage can enter marriage under the Special 
Marriage Act, 1954. Further, certain person al laws also deal with this issue. 
For example, section 8 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1995 provides that for the 
purpose of facilitating the proof of Hindu marriages, the State Government 
may make rules providing that the parties to any such marriage may have the

such conditions as may be prescribed in a Hindu Marriage Register kept for 
the purpose. Section 37 of the Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1872 provides 
that marriage between Indian Christians shall be registered . Section 6 of the 
Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act, 1936 also provides that every marriage 
under that Act shall be registered. Some of the State Governments have made 
law for uniform compulsory regPstration of marriages.

registration of mafriages by 2010.

UPON hearing counsel the Court made the following 
ORDER 
We have heard the learned counsel for the petitioner. The challenge is to the 
validity of the petitioner. The challenge is to the validity of the legal services 
authority (Amendment) Act, 2002 (in short the 'Act') whereby a new Chapter 
6(A) has been inserted relating to pre-litigation conciliation and settlement. It 
is quite apparent that this chapter has been enacted as being complementary to 
Section 89 of the code of civil Procedure, 1908 (in short the 'Code') which is a 
new provision enacted and implemented with effect from 1" July, 2002. 
We have gone through the provisions of the said Capter which contemplete 
the setting up of permanent Lok Adalats for deciding disputes in which 
public utility services is one of the matters involved. It is quite obvious that 
the effort of the legislature is to d ecrease the work load in the Courts by 
resorting to alternative disputes resolution. Lok Adalat is a mode of dispute 
resolution which has been in vogue since over two decades. Hundreds of 
thousands of cases have been set tled through this mechanism and is 
undisputedly a fast means of dispensation of justice. The litigation is brought 
to a quick end with no further appeals or anguish to the litigants. The 
constitution of the Perm anent Lok Adalats mech anism contemplate the 
judicial officer or a retired judicial officer being there aiongwith other 
persons having adequate experience in the public utility services. 
We do not find any constitutional infirmity in the said legislation. The Act 
ensures that justice will be available to the litigant speedily and impartially. 
We do emphasis that the persons who are appointed on the 
154 

[25 November, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Permanent Lok Adalats should be persons of integrity and adequate 
experience. Appropriate ru!es, inter alia in this regard, no doubt will have to 
be framed, if not already in place. 
We upheld the validity of the said Act and hope the "Permanent Lok 
Adalats will be set up at an early date. The Lok Adalats are enacted to 
primarily bring about settlement amongst the parties. The parties are normally 
required to be present in person and since the impugned provisions are in the 
interest of the litigating public, the Lok Adalats shall perform their duties and 
will function, even if members of the Bar choose not to appear." 
Petition is disposed of in the aforesaid terms. 
Copies of the order to be sent to the High Courts and also to the Attorney 
General.

Levy of user charges by States 
603. SHRl PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have asked States to levy user 
charges as part of an exercise to help States to augment resources for 
undertaking urban infrastructure projects; 
(b) whether this levy of user char ges is a precondition for accessing 
Central aid for urban reforms; and 
197 

RAJYA SABHA [25 November, 2002] 
(c) if so, the aims of this scheme and the objectives for which it is 
designed? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): 
(a) to (c) Urban Development is a State s ubject. It is, therefore, for the States 
to levy user charges to augment resources for undertaking urban 
infrastructure projects. However, in-order to accelerate the pace of sustainable 
urban development, Central Government announced the following new 
tools:— 
(i)   Urban Reforms Incentive Fund (URIF). 
(ii)   City Challenge Fund (CCF). 
(iii)   Pooled Finance Development Scheme (PFDS). 
URIF has been set up to provide reform  linked assistance to states in the 
following areas:— 
(i) Repeal of Urban Land Ceiling and Regulation Act at the State 
level by Resolution; 
(ii) Rationalization of Stamp Duty in phases to bring it down to no 
more than 5% by the end of the Tenth Plan period; 
(iii) Reform of Rent Control Laws to remove rent control so as to 
stimulate private investment in rental housing. 
(iv)   Introduction of computerized processes of registration; 
(v) Reform of Property Tax so that it may become a major source of 
revenue of urban local bodies, and arrangements for its effective 
implementation so that collection efficiency reaches at least 85% 
by the end of 10% Plan period; 
(vi) Levy of reasonable user charges by Urban Local Bodies with the 
objective that full cost of Oper ation & Maintenance is collected 
by the end of the Tenth Plan period; and 
(vii) Introduction of double entry sy stem of accounting in urban local 
bodies. 
CCF is an incentive based facility that will support cities to fund transitional 
costs of moving towards sustainable & creditworthy institutional systems of 
municipal management & service delivery. It will assist in the partial financing 
of the cost of developing an economic reform programme & financially viable 
projects to be undertaken by urban local bodies. 
198
